newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberians emerge from forest with tales of death.
newsitem.headline: Liberians emerge from forest with tales of death.

text.p: Thousands of civilians, cut off from relief aid by faction fighting for most of 1996, emerged from the forests and rubber plantations of south west Liberia with tales of death from lack of food and medicine.

As a U.N. food convoy dropped off food for 5,000 people in towns and villages in Cape Mount county for the first time in months on Friday, civilians and local aid workers said people had been dying each day in villages in the area.

Earlier, Charles Taylor, who launched the war in 1989 and whose faction was at the centre of fighting in the capital in April and May, said militia rivals had robbed and beaten his supporters who had tried to take food to Tubmanburg town.

"The death rate is very high in the area. I have recorded the total of 2,330 deaths in the whole of Garwula District over the last nine months," Folley Kiadi of the Liberians United to Serve Humanity (LUSH) group said in Vonzua.
"Even before the convoy arrived, three children died in (nearby) Bendu Town. I think the basic thing is lack of medicine," he added.
People in the area, which is plagued by malaria and other killer diseases, have subsistence food such as cassava but there were signs of malnutrition among many of the children.

West African peacekeepers ventured into Cape Mount for the first time since January on Monday. Two factions vying for control of the area agreed on Tuesday to grant relief groups unconditional safe passage for the first time in since March.

An assessment team, similar to one that discovered hundreds of starving children and old people in Tubmanburg this month, found malnourished people in five towns and related villages in Cape Mount on Wednesday. Relief trucks moved in on Friday.
Relief agencies believe that pockets of hungry Liberians may exist elsewhere in the country.
Well over 150,000 people have died in the civil war in Liberia, founded by freed American slaves in 1847.

West African leaders rallied faction leaders round a new peace deal in August and backed it with the threat of sanctions against anyone derailing the agreement. It envisages disarmament by January of next year and elections by May.

Taylor, a vice-chairman on the interim ruling State Council and a declared candidate for the election, said members of his team were beaten on the way to Tubmanburg by a rival ethnic Krahn militia and had their vehicles and relief items stolen.
In a statement, he added that the incident and the temporary seizure of two of his commanders during a truce monitoring mission this month would not affect his commitment to the peace process.
